title: What Does It Mean?
subtitle: People who love Piranesi often disagree about what it is really about. A strange book gives a group something real to argue over. How do you defend a reading without sounding certain, or giving it all away?

card.who: Susanna Clarke · Piranesi · readings and arguments
card.essence: A book that does not explain itself, and a group of readers who each see something different. How to build a reading from evidence and disagree politely.

intention: you'll talk about different readings of the book, use a three-step ladder to build and defend an interpretation, and practise the language of polite disagreement.
warmup: Think of a book, film or painting that people disagree about. What exactly do they disagree about?
Do you prefer stories that explain everything or stories that leave questions open? Why?
When you disagree with a friend about a book, what do you do?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The poem is deliberately ambiguous: it can be read as a love poem or as a poem about grief.
items.meaning: ambiguous (adjective) — having more than one possible meaning. Noun: ambiguity.

items.sent: Her interpretation of the ending was very different from mine, and she had good reasons for it.
items.meaning: interpretation (noun) — a particular way of understanding something. Verb: interpret.

items.sent: Many readers see the story as an allegory, in which the house stands for the human mind.
items.meaning: allegory (noun) — a story in which characters, places or events stand for deeper ideas, often moral or political ones.

items.sent: The final image resonated with me for weeks; I kept thinking about it long after I finished the book.
items.meaning: resonate (verb) — to continue to have meaning or emotional effect for someone. Adjective: resonant.

vocab.heading: B · Which term means…?
vocab.intro: Three terms: read into · come down on one side · agree to disagree. Say the right one, then reveal.

items.sent: Which term means to find a meaning in something that the author may not have intended?
items.meaning: read into — You are reading too much into one sentence.

items.sent: Which term means to decide that one view is better than the other after weighing both?
items.meaning: come down on one side — After a long discussion she came down on the side of the first reading.

items.sent: Which term means to accept that two people will never agree and to stop arguing about it?
items.meaning: agree to disagree — We could not settle it, so we agreed to disagree.

story_heading: A book that does not explain itself

story.heading: Part 1 — A strange book from an unexpected author
paras: Susanna Clarke was already well known for her first novel, Jonathan Strange and Mr Norrell, a long, witty book about magic in nineteenth-century England. Piranesi, published in 2020, is much shorter and stranger. It won the Women's Prize for Fiction in 2021 and found a large audience.

The title is the name that the narrator is given. It also points to a real person: Giovanni Battista Piranesi, an eighteenth-century Italian artist who made large, dramatic etchings of imaginary buildings, among them an enormous series of prisons with endless stairs and chambers.
That reference is useful because it sets the book's mood. The pictures are beautiful and a little frightening, and it is not always clear whether you are looking at a palace or a prison.
checks: Where does the title come from?
What mood does the reference create?
answers: A writer who was already famous for her first novel, a long book about magic in nineteenth-century England.
From the name the narrator is given, and from an eighteenth-century Italian artist who drew imaginary buildings.
Beautiful and a little frightening, with a palace that could also be a prison.
story.discuss: Have you ever looked at a picture and been unable to decide whether it was beautiful or frightening? What decided it?

story.heading: Part 2 — Some of the readings
paras: Readers have offered many ways of understanding the House. Some see it as a kind of heaven or sacred place, where attention to beauty is a form of prayer. Others see it as a prison dressed up as a gift, a place built to keep a person quiet. Some read it as an image of the mind, with its halls of memory and its tides of feeling. Others read it as a story about recovering from something harmful, or about how we look after the natural world.

None of these readings is the official one. The author does not say. Part of the book's character is that all of them can be defended with evidence from the text, and that each reader will feel one reading more strongly.
That is why the book is such a good one for a club. You are not trying to find the right answer. You are trying to make a good case and to listen to someone else's.
checks: Give two readings of the House.
Why is the book good for a club?
answers: Any two: a sacred place, a prison, the mind, a story about recovery, a comment on how we treat nature.
No. The author does not say.
Because each reading can be defended and the aim is a good argument, not the right answer.
story.discuss: Which reading appeals to you most, and which would you find hardest to accept?

story.heading: Part 3 — Arguing well
paras: A good discussion of a book like this follows a simple order. First, say what the text says. Second, say what points to your reading, one quotation, an image, a pattern. Third, say what you think it means. If you jump straight to the third step, the others may feel that you are only giving an opinion.

It is also useful to say what would change your mind. A reading that nothing could challenge is not a reading but a belief. And when someone disagrees, the best response is often a question: What in the text makes you say that?
At the end of a good meeting you may not agree. But you should be able to say, in your own words, what the other person's reading is and why a sensible person might hold it.
checks: What is the order of a good discussion?
What else is useful to say?
What should you be able to do at the end?
answers: Say what the text says, say what points to your reading, then say what it means.
Say the other person's reading in your own words and explain why a sensible person might hold it.
story.discuss: Have you ever changed your mind about a book because of a conversation? What did the other person say?

tool_tab.lead: A reading is only as good as the evidence for it. The Reading Ladder has three rungs, from bottom to top: text (what the book says), clue (what points to your idea) and reading (what you think it means). You build from the bottom and say each rung aloud.
how: Text: start with something concrete. The narrator says that the House is kind and that it provides for him.
Clue: choose what points to your reading. But he also never asks how he came to be there, and he is not able to leave.
Reading: now say what it means, with a hedge. I think this suggests that the House may be both a gift and a trap.
Invite the other view: finish with a question. What do you see in the same passage?

sort.intro: Each sentence is part of a discussion of the book. Which rung of the Reading Ladder is it?

items.text: The narrator names each hall after a statue it contains.
items.why: a fact from the book, with no interpretation.

items.text: This suggests that the House is a kind of mind.
items.why: it says what the details may mean.

items.text: He never asks how he arrived, and nobody answers the question for him.
items.why: it points to a pattern that supports a reading.

items.text: He writes his notes in a calm, orderly voice.
items.why: a plain description of what the narrator does.

items.text: I read the House as a place that keeps its occupant quiet.
The tides come in whenever the narrator is least prepared.
items.why: a detail the reader could use as evidence.

items.text: The other character visits twice a week.
It could be argued that the book is about attention as a form of love.

breaks: Reading too much into it. If one detail is carrying the whole argument, look for a second.
Treating a reading as the answer. Say I read it as, not it is.
Spoilers. In a group, say I'd like to talk about the ending, is that all right? before you start.
discuss: Which rung do you tend to skip, and what happens when you do?
Can a reading be wrong? What would make it a weak one?

grammar.name: Giving and defending an interpretation
grammar.lead: When you give a reading, the grammar signals how strongly you hold it. A few expressions let you be confident without sounding as if you were stating a fact.
notes: Hedged interpretation: It could be argued that… This seems to suggest that… I would read it as… One way of looking at it is that… Each one tells the listener that you are offering a view.
Pointing to evidence: I would point to the way he… What makes me say that is… The detail that stands out for me is… Introduce the clue before the claim.

Polite disagreement: I see what you mean, but I read it differently. That is an interesting point. I am not sure I would go as far as that. What in the text makes you say that? Acknowledge first, then add your view.

exercises.heading: Which phrase?
exercises.intro: Complete each sentence with a phrase from the box. Use each once: could be argued · would point to · see what you mean · not sure I would go.
items: 1. It ___ that the House is a form of protection.
2. I ___ the way he never asks where he came from.
3. I ___ , but I read the scene differently.
4. I am ___ as far as saying he is a prisoner.
answers: 3. see what you mean — acknowledges the other view
4. not sure I would go — a polite limit

exercises.heading: Disagree politely
exercises.intro: Write one word in each gap.
items: 1. That is an interesting ___ , but I read the scene differently. (a thing someone has said that is worth thinking about)
2. I am not ___ I agree. What in the book makes you say that?
3. I see ___ you mean, but I would read it another way.
4. One way of ___ at it is that the House is a kind of prison.
answers: 2. sure — I am not sure I agree
4. looking — one way of looking at it

grammar.closing: Now give your own reading of the book in four sentences. Use a text, a clue and a hedged reading, and invite another view.

speak.intro: Choose a task, start the timer and talk. On your own it works as a talk; with a partner or a group, take turns and respond to each other.
speak.useful: “It could be argued that…” · “I would point to…” · “I see what you mean, but…” · “What in the book makes you say that?” · “I read it as…”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Your reading
paras: Give your reading of the book in one minute. Climb the ladder: say what the book says, what points to your idea, and what you think it means.

tasks.label: Task 2 — The other side
paras: Choose a reading that you do not hold. Present it as fairly as you can, with evidence. Then say what makes you prefer your own.

tasks.label: Task 3 — Disagree well
paras: Your partner gives a reading that you find hard to accept. Respond politely, ask what in the book makes them say that, and say one thing you agree with.

final: Does it matter what the author meant? Is there a right reading of a book?
Are books that leave questions open better than books that answer them?
What is the difference between disagreeing with a reading and disagreeing with a person?
